justice: The presence of paved sidewalks on both sides demonstrates a basic equitable distribution of walking space for general pedestrians
The lack of visible tactile paving (blind tracks) along the right sidewalk significantly reduces fairness and navigability for visually impaired users
The exceptionally wide zebra crossing lacks a central pedestrian refuge island, reducing accessibility and making crossing difficult for older adults or mobility-impaired individuals
safety: The wide, multi-lane road design encourages vehicle speeding without visible traffic calming measures, posing severe risks to teenagers and older adults
While a prominent zebra crossing provides clear right-of-way, the absence of pedestrian traffic signals increases crossing hazards

livability: The absence of street-level commercial storefronts or amenities limits daily convenience for nearby residents
Sparse pedestrian activity and a lack of active frontages result in poor 'eyes on the street' social surveillance, which can make teenagers and vulnerable groups feel isolated
There are no visible community gathering spaces, plazas, or interactive facilities for older adults or teenagers to socialize
sustainability: Street trees and roadside vegetation strips are present, contributing to basic urban greening and carbon absorption
The street is dominated by impermeable asphalt surfaces with no visible rainwater infiltration systems like rain gardens or bioswales
The provision of a dedicated non-motorized vehicle lane supports low-carbon travel alternatives such as cycling
aesthetics: The street surface is notably clean with highly visible, well-maintained white lane markings that provide a neat visual appearance
The architectural contrast between traditional white-walled structures on the left and modern commercial buildings on the right adds visual interest

comfort: Young, sparse street trees provide almost no canopy shade over the sidewalks, leading to poor thermal comfort for elderly pedestrians during hot weather
The complete absence of street benches or resting facilities forces older adults to walk long distances without physical relief
The flat, unobstructed asphalt surface in the non-motorized lane offers a physically smooth and comfortable ride for cyclists and mobility scooters
The wide open spatial layout and proximity to heavy traffic likely expose pedestrians to significant psychological discomfort from traffic noise and exposure
walkability: Wide, unobstructed paved sidewalks on the right allow sufficient space for wheelchairs and strollers to navigate easily
The continuous, excessively long zebra crossing without a midway resting point is physically exhausting for slower-moving elderly pedestrians
The lack of engaging street facades, combined with insufficient shade, makes walking along this corridor visually monotonous and physically unappealing for all users
bikeability: A clearly marked non-motorized vehicle lane exists on the right side, actively accommodating the tricycle and other cyclists seen in the image
The lack of a physical buffer (such as planters or bollards) between the bike lane and motor vehicle lanes reduces perceived and actual safety for teenage and elderly cyclists
